decisions.decision: There is exactly ONE correlation identifier, `requestId`, and it is a valid W3C trace-id (32 lowercase hex chars). When OTel is enabled the edge adopts `trace.getActiveSpan().spanContext().traceId` as the requestId; when OTel is off it is `randomBytes(16).toString('hex')`. The same 32 chars appear in every log line, the `x-request-id` response header, the metric exemplar `trace_id`, the `audit_event.request_id` column, the JSON-RPC `error.data.requestId` returned to the MCP client, and as a mono chip on every UI row.
decisions.rationale: A separate requestId and traceId means every join is two-keyed and one of them is always missing. Making them the same value costs one conditional at the edge and deletes the whole class of 'I have the log line but not the trace' problems. Returning it in the JSON-RPC error means a user of Claude Code can paste an id at the operator, who pastes it into one search box.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has neither. No request ID anywhere, no tracing, and the activity row cannot be joined to a log line because the logs are a console monkey-patch with no structured fields (logService.ts:70,115-153). Their docs punt to an external APM, which cannot correlate either because nothing emits an id.

decisions.decision: Propagation is `AsyncLocalStorage` from `node:async_hooks`, owned by `packages/core/src/obs/context.ts`. `packages/server` calls `runWithContext(ctx, handler)` as the outermost middleware; core reads `currentContext()`. Only `.run()` is ever used — `.enterWith()` is banned by an eslint `no-restricted-properties` rule. The store object is mutable in place so the auth middleware can set `ctx.principal` after the run has begun, and there is exactly one writer per field.
decisions.rationale: Rung 3 of the ladder: stdlib already does context propagation. The engine never imports the HTTP layer because the dependency arrow points the other way — core owns the ALS, server imports it. Core APIs stay 'given a resolved scope and principal, do X'; the context is ambient telemetry, never an argument the engine's signatures depend on.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub uses AsyncLocalStorage for the principal but ships an `enterWith` fallback (userContextService.ts:28,38) that can leak a principal across async boundaries — a cross-user authorization bug wearing a telemetry costume. Same primitive, one banned method, bug gone.

decisions.decision: Correlation reaches log lines through pino's `mixin` option, not through `log.child()` plumbing. The root logger's mixin reads the ALS and injects `{req, usr, key, scope, srv}` into every line. No call site in core or server ever passes a correlation field by hand.
decisions.rationale: One function on the logger config replaces threading a child logger through every engine signature. If the mixin is the only path, it cannot be forgotten, and engine code can keep calling the module-level `log` like it is 2015.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub monkey-patches global `console.*` and scrapes the formatted string for a `[server]` prefix (logService.ts:115-153). Every log line is unstructured text, so the log view filters by substring and nothing can be grouped.

decisions.decision: Secrets are kept out of logs by pino `serializers` on domain objects, not by regex scrubbing and not mainly by `redact` paths. `serializers.server = redactServerConfig` returns `{name,type,url,command,envKeys:string[],headerKeys:string[]}` — key names only, never values — so even a careless `log.info({server: cfg})` is safe. `redact` covers the fixed HTTP header paths (`*.authorization`, `*.cookie`, `*.["x-api-key"]`, `*.accessToken`, `*.refreshToken`, `*.clientSecret`). Tool arguments and tool results are NEVER logged at any level — a log line gets `inBytes`, `outBytes` and `inHash` (sha256 first 16 hex).
decisions.rationale: `redact` is path-based and silently misses a secret that arrives under an unexpected key. A serializer is type-directed: it is impossible to log the object without it running. And hashing arguments instead of logging them gives you 'these 400 failures are all the same call' without holding one byte of customer data.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub stores `env` and `headers` in plaintext in mcp_settings.json and JSON columns, and OAuth access/refresh tokens plaintext (oauthSettingsStore.ts:107-129). There is no log redaction at all; anything a `console.log` touches lands in the ring and streams to the browser.

decisions.decision: The dashboard's live log view is fed by a SECOND pino destination: `pino.multistream([{stream: process.stdout}, {stream: ring, level: 'debug'}])`, where `ring` is a bounded 2000-entry array of parsed records with cursor-based subscribers. `GET /api/logs/stream` (Hono `streamSSE`) hands each subscriber a cursor into the ring; a slow client that falls behind the oldest entry gets one `{evt:'logs.dropped', n}` frame and jumps forward. There are no per-subscriber buffers and there is no monkey-patch.
decisions.rationale: The ring IS the queue; subscriber backpressure is a cursor comparison, which is the entire slow-consumer story for free. Writing to a Writable is pino's documented extension point, so we get the identical JSON the operator sees in `docker logs`, not a parallel reality.
decisions.cost: ~95 LOC for ring.ts, ~95 for the route
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub monkey-patches `console.*` into a 1000-entry ring (logService.ts:70), streams it at `/api/logs/stream` with the JWT IN THE QUERY STRING (frontend services/logService.ts:82), has no server-side level filter, and LogViewer renders every entry from an unbounded array. We use the better-auth session cookie — EventSource sends cookies automatically, so the token never enters a URL, and we keep a hard cap of 20 concurrent subscribers.

decisions.decision: Default log sink is stdout NDJSON and nothing else. `pino-roll` is wired only when `LOG_FILE` is set (bare-metal/systemd self-host): daily rotation, `size:'50m'`, `limit:{count:14}`, `mkdir:true`. Dev uses the `pino-pretty` transport target, a devDependency, selected by `NODE_ENV!=='production'`.
decisions.rationale: Rung 1: does file rotation need to exist? In Docker and k8s, no — the json-file driver and the kubelet already rotate and retain. Shipping our own rotation by default would be re-implementing the platform. One env var covers the minority who run bare node.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has no file sink, no rotation and no retention at all — logs exist only in the 1000-entry ring and vanish on restart. We keep the container path free and give the bare-metal path a real answer.

decisions.decision: OpenTelemetry is OPT-IN, configured entirely by the standard `OTEL_*` env vars, enabled iff `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` (or the traces-specific variant) is set. Bootstrap is an unconditional `node --import ./otel-bootstrap.mjs dist/index.js` whose first line is `if (!endpoint) return;`. We do NOT install `@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node`. We install exactly three: `instrumentation-http`, `instrumentation-pg`, `instrumentation-undici`. Traces only — no OTel metrics pipeline, no OTel logs pipeline. `packages/core` depends on `@opentelemetry/api` ONLY (a no-op without an SDK); `@opentelemetry/sdk-node` is a `packages/server` dependency.
decisions.rationale: auto-instrumentations-node pulls ~40 instrumentation packages to give us three things we actually want. Naming those three is a smaller dependency tree, a faster boot, and an audit surface a human can read. Everything MCP-specific — tool call, upstream connect, vector search — no instrumentation could ever know, so it is hand-written regardless. One signal per tool: Prometheus owns metrics, pino owns logs, OTel owns traces, and none of them half-owns another.
decisions.cost: ~45 LOC bootstrap, ~70 LOC withSpan helper + attribute constants
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has no OpenTelemetry, no tracing and no request-ID correlation; their docs admit it and defer to an external APM that has nothing to consume. The contrast here is not 'we added OTel', it is 'we added the 5% of OTel that answers a question'.

decisions.decision: Cardinality rule, enforced mechanically: never multiply two medium-cardinality dimensions inside one metric. `tool` appears as a label on COUNTERS only (`mcprouter_tool_calls_total{server,tool,outcome}`), never on a histogram. Caller identity appears in a SEPARATE counter (`mcprouter_client_calls_total{client,outcome}`, where `client` is the better-auth apiKey id — admin-created, bounded — never the client-supplied `clientInfo.name`). Per-(tool × client × latency) detail lives in Postgres. The `tool` label value is typed: `recordToolCall(ref: ResolvedTool | null, ...)` takes a branded resolved-tool object, and a `null` ref records `tool="__unknown__"` — so a client hammering nonexistent tool names cannot mint series.
decisions.rationale: The trap is not the tool label per se, it is (a) unbounded input reaching a label and (b) crossing tool × client × bucket. 1200 tools on a counter is 3600 series and fine; 1200 tools on a 13-bucket histogram is 45k and not. Types do the enforcing so nobody has to remember the rule.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has no /metrics endpoint at all, so it has no cardinality policy to get wrong — and no way to alert on anything. This is the differentiator: a metrics surface designed by someone who has been paged by a cardinality explosion.

decisions.decision: Metric exemplars carry the trace id natively via prom-client 15's `enableExemplars`, on `mcprouter_tool_call_duration_seconds` and `mcprouter_tool_calls_total` only. `/metrics` negotiates: if the scrape `Accept` header contains `application/openmetrics-text`, the registry serializes with `Registry.OPENMETRICS_CONTENT_TYPE` and exemplars are included; otherwise plain Prometheus text.
decisions.rationale: Rung 5 — the installed dependency already does exemplars, we just pass `exemplarLabels:{trace_id: ctx.requestId}` from the ALS. Content negotiation is four lines and means a scraper that does not understand OpenMetrics is not broken by us.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: N/A — mcphub emits no metrics. Worth stating because 'click the latency spike, land in the trace' is the single feature that makes a metrics page worth opening.

decisions.decision: Audit payload policy has three modes — `off` | `metadata` (DEFAULT) | `full` — settable globally and overridable per server. `metadata` stores argument KEY NAMES (`input_keys text[]`), byte counts and hashes, never values. `full` stores input and output VERBATIM with no heuristic scrubbing (we AGREE with mcphub that a regex redactor is false confidence), capped at 64 KB each with a `{"__truncated":true,"bytes":N}` marker. We DISAGREE with mcphub on the default: verbatim-on-by-default turns the audit table into the highest-value target in the deployment. `full` is made survivable by three separate controls: payload columns are nulled at `AUDIT_PAYLOAD_RETENTION_DAYS` (default 7) while metadata rows live to `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS` (default 90); reading a payload requires the distinct `audit:payload:read` permission; and every payload read writes its own audit row (`evt:'audit.payload.read'`). Calls that used a per-user credential binding are metadata-only ALWAYS, with no override.
decisions.rationale: mcphub's reasoning is right and their conclusion is wrong. Heuristic redaction does miss the secret in a field called `q` and does mangle real data — so do not redact. But 'therefore store everything forever by default' does not follow. Default to the mode that answers 95% of audit questions (who called what, how often, with which argument shape) at near-zero blast radius, and make the dangerous mode explicit, short-lived, separately permissioned and self-auditing.
decisions.cost: ~70 LOC of the audit module + 1 migration column
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub stores tool input and output VERBATIM by design, on by default, opt out via `activityLog.storeToolPayload`, 100 KB cap, retention is a MANUAL `DELETE /api/activities/cleanup?daysOld=` an operator must remember to call (activityLoggingService.ts:112-118,:142). We keep their no-heuristics principle, invert the default, split the retention clocks, and make cleanup automatic.

decisions.decision: Audit writes are off the tool-call critical path: a bounded in-process queue (cap 10 000) flushed by one writer on a 250 ms tick or at 200 rows, using a single multi-row INSERT. If the flush fails, the batch is re-queued once; if the DB stays down and the queue fills, each evicted record is emitted to the LOG stream at `error` with `evt:'audit.spill'` and the full record as JSON, so it lands in stdout/Docker logs rather than vanishing. `mcprouter_audit_dropped_total` and `mcprouter_audit_write_failures_total` make it visible. SIGTERM triggers a synchronous flush with a 5 s budget.
decisions.rationale: A synchronous insert per tool call puts Postgres on the latency path and turns a DB blip into a gateway outage. Spilling to stdout converts silent loss into recoverable loss for ~6 lines, which is the difference between an acceptable corner-cut and a compliance incident. Marked in-code: `ponytail: at-most-once audit under sustained DB failure; upgrade to an on-disk spool if at-least-once is required`.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub's activity logging is DB-mode only (activityLoggingService.ts:38-40) and simply does not exist in JSON mode — a whole deployment mode with no audit trail. We have one storage mode, so audit is unconditional.

decisions.decision: Three distinct health surfaces with three distinct contracts. `GET /healthz` (liveness, unauthenticated) returns 200 iff the event loop runs — it NEVER inspects a dependency, because killing the container will not fix Postgres. `GET /readyz` (readiness, unauthenticated) returns 200 only when migrations are applied, `SELECT 1` succeeds inside 2 s, the first upstream reconciliation pass has completed and the MCP routes are mounted; otherwise 503 with per-check booleans and NO server names or version strings. Upstream MCP server state is deliberately NOT part of readiness. `GET /api/health/fleet` (authenticated) always returns 200 and is a REPORT, not a probe: per-server state, since, lastError, lastSuccessAt, p95 and 5-minute error rate. The word 'degraded' exists only in the fleet report and never in a probe status code.
decisions.rationale: The three questions are 'should I restart you', 'should I send you traffic' and 'is the fleet healthy'. Conflating the last two means one broken third-party MCP server pulls a working router out of the load balancer; conflating the first two means a Postgres hiccup starts a restart loop. Also: an unauthenticated probe that enumerates your upstream servers is free reconnaissance.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has one `GET /health`, unauthenticated, 503 on DB failure and 200 'degraded' when upstreams are down (healthController.ts:32-46) — a naive probe passes a hub whose every upstream is dead, and the same endpoint leaks fleet state to anyone who can reach the port.

interfaces.name: RequestContext + propagation
interfaces.notes: This is the whole propagation story. The engine never imports the HTTP layer; it calls currentContext(). When OTel is disabled @opentelemetry/api returns undefined for getActiveSpan() and the fallback runs — no branch, no config.

interfaces.name: Structured log shape + event vocabulary
interfaces.notes: Levels: trace=off in prod; debug=per-request engine detail; info=lifecycle + one access line per request; warn=retry/degraded/upstream stderr; error=failed call, failed connect, audit spill; fatal=process exiting. `evt` is what the UI filters on and what an operator greps.

interfaces.name: LogRing — bounded ring with cursor subscribers
interfaces.notes: The ring is the queue. Subscribers hold an integer, not a buffer, so a stalled browser tab costs nothing and slow-consumer handling is one comparison. Cap is a constant, not config — upgrade path is to point the UI at Loki, not to grow the array.

interfaces.name: Prometheus metric catalogue — every metric, type, labels, cardinality
interfaces.notes: Rule stated once: never multiply two medium-cardinality dimensions in one metric — emit two metrics and join in Postgres. Prometheus answers 'what shape is the fleet'; the audit table answers 'who exactly'. Exemplars are on tool_calls_total and tool_call_duration_seconds only, via prom-client's enableExemplars + Registry.OPENMETRICS_CONTENT_TYPE when the scrape Accept header asks for it.

interfaces.name: OTel spans and attributes
interfaces.notes: Seven manual spans, three named instrumentations, zero auto-instrumentation meta-package. A tool call under load produces: http server span -> mcp.request -> mcp.tool.call -> mcp.upstream.call (-> undici span), plus any pg spans. That is the whole fan-out of a request on one screen.

interfaces.name: audit_event (Drizzle + migration)
interfaces.notes: One table, not two. mcphub's Activity entity has the same spine but no upstream_ms (so you cannot separate 'the upstream is slow' from 'we are slow'), no request_id (so nothing joins to a log line), and no input_keys mode between verbatim and nothing.

interfaces.name: HTTP route table
interfaces.notes: Every MCP error response also carries error.data.requestId, so a user can paste an id at an operator who pastes it into /api/observability/request/:requestId and sees the audit row, every log line and a deep link to the trace.

interfaces.name: GET /api/observability/triage — the operator query
interfaces.sketch:
-- "Which upstream is slow or failing right now, and which client is causing it?"
-- ONE query. Served by GET /api/observability/triage?window=15m. Index: audit_server_at_idx.
WITH w AS (
  SELECT server, outcome, upstream_ms, duration_ms,
         coalesce(api_key_id, principal_id, client_name, 'anon') AS caller
  FROM audit_event
  WHERE at > now() - ($1::text)::interval AND server IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT server,
       count(*)                                                     AS calls,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome <> 'ok')                      AS errors,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome <> 'ok')
             / nullif(count(*),0), 1)                               AS error_pct,
       percentile_disc(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY upstream_ms)    AS p50_upstream_ms,
       percentile_disc(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY upstream_ms)    AS p95_upstream_ms,
       max(upstream_ms)                                             AS max_upstream_ms,
       percentile_disc(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_ms)
         - percentile_disc(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY upstream_ms) AS p95_router_overhead_ms,
       mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY caller)                        AS top_caller,
       count(DISTINCT caller)                                       AS callers
FROM w GROUP BY server
ORDER BY p95_upstream_ms DESC NULLS LAST, errors DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Drill 1 (click a server row): same window, GROUP BY caller, ORDER BY p95 DESC.
-- Drill 2 (click a call): request_id -> /api/observability/request/:id ->
--          { audit row, every log line with that req, trace deep link }.
-- Live half of the same screen, no DB: mcprouter_tool_calls_inflight and
--   histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (server,le) (rate(
--     mcprouter_tool_call_duration_seconds_bucket{phase="upstream"}[5m])))
--   for the last-60s shape the 15-minute SQL window cannot see.
interfaces.notes: Postgres does the who (unbounded dimensions, exact percentiles); Prometheus does the right-now shape (5-second resolution). The screen is one table of upstreams sorted by p95, a sparkline per row from the Prometheus range query, a top_caller column, and a click-through to the exact request. mcphub cannot render this: its Activity rows record duration but not the upstream/total split, and there is no aggregation endpoint at all.

interfaces.name: Engine and server contracts (what I need from the other seven)
interfaces.notes: Hooks are a plain object on the engine, not an event emitter and not an interface with two implementations. One implementation, injected once at boot; tests pass a recording stub.

interfaces.name: Environment variables
interfaces.sketch:
LOG_LEVEL=info                      # trace|debug|info|warn|error|fatal
LOG_FILE=                           # unset => stdout only (Docker/k8s rotate for us).
                                    # set => pino-roll daily, size 50m, keep 14.
AUDIT_PAYLOADS=metadata             # off | metadata | full   (per-server override in server config)
AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS=90             # metadata rows
AUDIT_PAYLOAD_RETENTION_DAYS=7      # payload columns nulled first, separate clock
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=        # unset => OTel bootstrap returns on line 1, zero cost
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=mcprouter
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_always_on
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=
OTEL_TRACE_URL_TEMPLATE=            # e.g. https://grafana.example/explore?traceID={traceId}
                                    # one string replace; no vendor SDK, no dependency
# NOT env vars, deliberately: ring size (constant 2000), metric prefix, bucket layouts,
# SSE keep-alive interval, audit batch size. No config for a value that never changes.
interfaces.notes: Everything OTel is a STANDARD OTEL_* name so an operator's existing collector config drops in. The only MCPRouter-specific OTel variable is the UI deep-link template.

interfaces.name: Web: LogStream / TriagePanel / RequestDrawer
interfaces.notes: mcphub's LogViewer is one global firehose over an unbounded array with no per-server filter and uses emoji as status (StatusDot.tsx:67,83). Server-side filtering plus a fixed client cap is less code than their client-side filtering and does not melt the tab.

vitest + @testcontainers/postgresql: batch insert, 64KB truncation marker, metadata mode stores keys not values, credentialed forces metadata, spill-to-log on DB down, retention nulls then deletes.

security: Inbound `traceparent` header (downstream HTTP -> context). Untrusted. Control: strict regex `^00-(?!0{32})([0-9a-f]{32})-[0-9a-f]{16}-[0-9a-f]{2}$`; anything that fails generates a fresh id. Prevents trace-id injection, log-field forging, and a client grafting its requests onto someone else's trace.

Client-supplied identity strings (`clientInfo.name`/`version`, `Mcp-Name` header). Untrusted. Control: stored in audit only, never used as a metric label, capped at 128/64 chars, control characters and newlines stripped before they reach the ring or the UI. NDJSON escaping already stops log forging on the stdout path; the cap protects the SPA render path and the table.

Tool names reaching a Prometheus label. Untrusted when unresolved. Control: `recordToolCall` accepts only a branded `ResolvedTool` from the registry; a null ref records `tool="__unknown__"`. A client that calls 10 000 nonexistent tool names creates one series, not 10 000. This is a denial-of-service control, not a tidiness rule.

`GET /metrics`. Control: better-auth apiKey `permissions` requires `metrics:read`, or an admin session. Never public — the metric set enumerates every upstream server name, every tool name and the full traffic shape of the organisation.

`GET /api/logs` and `/api/logs/stream`. Control: better-auth session cookie ONLY (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax), admin role required. No credential may be passed in the query string — mcphub puts the JWT in the log-stream URL (frontend services/logService.ts:82), which copies it into every reverse-proxy access log and browser history entry. EventSource sends cookies automatically, so this costs nothing. Responses carry `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no`; concurrent subscribers capped at 20.

Secrets reaching a log line. Control: pino `serializers` is type-directed and cannot be bypassed by a careless call site — `serializers.server` emits `envKeys`/`headerKeys`, never values. `redact` covers the fixed header/token paths. Tool arguments, tool results, resource bodies, prompt bodies and embedding query text are NEVER logged at any level; log lines carry byte counts and a sha256 prefix instead.

Audit payload columns (`full` mode). Control: three independent gates — a distinct `audit:payload:read` permission separate from `audit:read`; admin session required; and every read writes its own audit row (`evt:'audit.payload.read'` with the target row id). Payloads are nulled at 7 days by default while metadata survives 90. Calls that used a per-user credential binding are metadata-only with no override, reproducing mcphub's credentialed-call rule (activityLoggingService.ts:70-75) as an unconditional invariant rather than a flag that fails open for any new auth path.

`/healthz` and `/readyz` are unauthenticated by necessity (probes). Control: response bodies contain check names and booleans only — no upstream server names, no version string, no error text. mcphub's unauthenticated `/health` reports degraded fleet state to anyone who can reach the port (healthController.ts:32-46).

Audit write loss. Control: bounded queue with a re-queue-once retry; when the DB is unreachable, each evicted record is emitted to the log stream at `error` with `evt:'audit.spill'` and the full record, so it lands in stdout/Docker logs instead of vanishing. `mcprouter_audit_dropped_total` and `mcprouter_audit_write_failures_total` are page-worthy at any nonzero value.

Observability must not undo the hidden-tool contract. `mcprouter_tool_denied_total{reason}` and `audit_event.outcome='denied'` record the distinction between a disabled tool and a nonexistent one, but the JSON-RPC error code and message returned to the client remain byte-identical for both (mcphub's ToolUnavailableError, mcpService.ts:2654). No observability field may leak into a client-visible response except `error.data.requestId`, which is an opaque random value.

deferred.add_when: We need spans inside a dependency we do not control and cannot wrap ourselves — e.g. a redis or S3 client appears in the tree. Adding one named instrumentation stays cheaper than the meta-package until we need four or more.

Someone actually runs Grafana against us. Our TriagePanel answers the primary question in-product; a dashboard is a second thing to keep in sync.
A deployment starts billing or rate-limiting per group. Until then group is a filter in the SQL, not a metric dimension.

deferred.item: Tail-based sampling / a span processor that keeps only error traces.
deferred.add_when: Trace volume becomes a cost line. `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` head sampling is the first, free answer.

deferred.item: Anomaly detection / baseline alerting on upstream p95.
deferred.add_when: Someone complains that static thresholds in alerts.yml page too often. A static threshold that pages is still better than a clever one nobody trusts.
A customer asks for an auditor deliverable. It is one streaming SELECT; not worth building speculatively.

risks: The requestId-is-the-trace-id trick depends on the `mcp.request` span existing before the context is created. If a future middleware reorder puts auth or routing ahead of the span, log lines silently lose OTel correlation while still having an id — a failure with no error. Mitigation: one test asserts that with the SDK registered, a log line's `req` equals the exported span's traceId.

The RequestContext store is mutable in place so auth can set `principal` late. If a second writer appears (e.g. a retry path resetting `server`), audit rows and log lines can disagree about which upstream handled a call. Mitigation: fields are documented single-writer and the engine sets `server` exactly once, at resolution; a retry to a different transport on the same server does not change it.

`mcprouter_context_tokens` is the one metric where I deliberately accept ~1000 series. A deployment with 500 servers and 200 groups pushes past 2800 and a scrape starts costing real time. The ceiling and the fix (drop the `scope` label, keep the SQL view) are written down, but nobody will notice until the scrape times out.

The `--import ./otel-bootstrap.mjs` preload with import-in-the-middle is the least boring part of the design and the part most likely to break on a Node minor bump under pure ESM. Mitigation: the bootstrap's first line returns when no OTLP endpoint is set, so the default deployment never loads the hook at all — a breakage can only affect operators who opted in, and it degrades to 'no traces', not 'no boot'.

Async batched audit writes mean a tool call can succeed and its audit row can be lost if the process is SIGKILLed inside the 250 ms window. SIGTERM flushes; SIGKILL and OOM do not. For a compliance deployment this is the wrong tradeoff and the upgrade path (synchronous insert, or an on-disk spool) is a real change, not a flag.

`metadata` as the default payload mode will produce at least one incident where the operator needed the arguments and only has the key names. The per-server `full` override exists precisely for that, but it has to be turned on BEFORE the incident. Mitigation: the RequestDrawer shows a one-click 'enable full payloads for this server' affordance with the 7-day retention stated inline.

JSON.parse per log line in the ring is fine at hundreds/sec and not fine at tens of thousands. A debug-level flood from one chatty stdio upstream's stderr is the realistic trigger. Mitigation: the ring is attached at `debug`, `LOG_LEVEL` defaults to `info`, and upstream stderr is rate-limited to 20 lines/sec/server before it reaches pino.

prom-client exemplars require the OpenMetrics content type, which some scrape stacks (and most alertmanager-only setups) do not negotiate. Those operators get correct metrics with no exemplars and may conclude the trace linking is broken. Mitigation: the /metrics response includes a comment line naming the required Accept header, and the docs say it in one sentence.

Cookie-only auth on /api/logs/stream means the log view does not work from a CLI or a cross-origin dashboard. That is deliberate, but it will be reported as a bug. `mcprouter logs --follow` in the CLI must use `GET /api/logs` polling with an API key, not the SSE endpoint — a contract the CLI subsystem has to honour.
phase: "Phase 1 (with the core+server skeleton, before any MCP traffic flows): context.ts, log.ts, ring.ts, /healthz, /readyz, the request middleware, the metrics registry with downstream + upstream + db-pool families. Depends on: packages/server's middleware chain existing; the auth subsystem's Principal type (can start with `principal: null`); the db subsystem's Pool handle. Nothing here depends on the engine being finished. Phase 2 (as soon as tool calls execute end to end): audit_event migration, the audit queue + retention timer, tool-call and denial metrics, the triage endpoint, otel-bootstrap and the seven spans. Depends on: the engine's EngineObsHooks call sites, and the auth subsystem having shipped the metrics:read / audit:read / audit:payload:read permissions on the better-auth apiKey plugin. Phase 3 (with the web SPA): LogStream, TriagePanel, FleetHealth, RequestDrawer, the context-cost and embedding gauges (these depend on the Context Cost and Smart Routing subsystems calling onContextTokens/onVectorSearch), and deploy/prometheus/alerts.yml. The `mcprouter_sessions_active` gauge is born in Phase 2 and is marked for deletion the day the SDK ships 2026-07-28 support — it is the only piece of this subsystem with a known expiry date."
subsystem: "Observability — structured logging, correlation, tracing, metrics, audit trail, health"
summary: "One correlation id, generated once at the HTTP edge and equal to the W3C trace-id, carried through the engine by a stdlib AsyncLocalStorage that packages/core owns, so the engine never imports the HTTP layer. That id is injected into every pino line by a `mixin` (no child-logger plumbing), attached to metric exemplars by prom-client's native OpenMetrics support, written to every audit row, returned in the `x-request-id` header and in `error.data.requestId`, and rendered as a copyable chip on every UI row. Secrets stay out of logs by type-directed pino `serializers` rather than regex scrubbing, and tool payloads never reach a log line at all — only byte counts and a hash. The single idea that makes this leaner than mcphub is a hard split of responsibility: Prometheus answers 'what shape is the fleet right now' with strictly bounded label sets, Postgres answers 'who exactly did what' with one SQL query and unbounded dimensions, and the two are joined by that one id — so there is no per-tool histogram, no cardinality bomb, no log pipeline to run, and the operator's real question is answered by one table and one statement. mcphub has a monkey-patched 1000-entry console ring, a DB-only activity table with no upstream/total latency split and no request id, no /metrics, no tracing, and a /health that returns 200 'degraded' while every upstream is down."
